title: Astronomers discover that asteroid Bennu doesn't fit into any category (and Jupiter may be to blame)
excerpt: Bennu reveals where it formed: Its samples contain a mixture of materials from the inner and outer solar system dating back 4.5 billion years.
content:
Asteroid Bennu holds a kind of time capsule within it. Its materials have remained virtually unchanged since the earliest days of the solar system, and now, thanks to samples collected by NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission, scientists have been able to reconstruct part of the story of its formation.

Bennu completes one orbit around the Sun every 1.2 years and approaches Earth approximately every six years, passing at a distance of about 300,000 kilometers. This proximity allowed NASA to send a mission to its surface and collect material directly from the asteroid.

In September 2023, the capsule carrying the samples landed in the Utah desert. Inside were approximately 120 grams of material from Bennu. A small portion, just half a gram, was later delivered to the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich (ETH Zurich), where a team led by isotope geochemist Maria Schönbächler began studying it.

The findings have just been published in the journal Science Advances and provide another piece of the puzzle in understanding how planets formed.

A chemical fingerprint linking Bennu to other celestial bodies

Researchers analyzed the iron, titanium, and chromium isotopes found in the samples. These atoms belong to the same chemical elements but differ slightly in mass. Their particular combination acts as a unique fingerprint that can reveal the origin of a celestial body.

The analyses showed that titanium and iron are uniformly distributed throughout Bennu. They also revealed an unexpected connection.

The asteroid shares a remarkably similar isotopic signature with Ryugu, another primitive asteroid visited by a Japanese space mission, and with meteorites known as CI chondrites, which are extremely ancient and rich in carbon. All three appear to have formed from the same reservoir of cosmic dust.

However, its composition is clearly different from that of other known asteroids, meteorite groups, and planets.

Bennu formed where two regions of the solar system met

For years, scientists had suggested that Bennu and similar asteroids might have formed in the outer regions of the solar system, possibly near the area where comets originated. They also believed these objects had formed relatively late.

The new findings point in a different direction. The most likely scenario places the formation of Bennu, Ryugu, and CI meteorites near what is known as the water snow line. This is a region of the disk surrounding the young Sun where water could transition from vapor to ice.

About 4.5 billion years ago, when the solar system was still taking shape, materials from its inner and outer regions mixed in this area. Ice may also have played a fundamental role, acting as a kind of glue that bound the finest dust particles together.

"Bennu is a hybrid," explains Schönbächler. Its composition does not fully match that of either the inner or outer solar system but instead displays characteristics of both.

Jupiter's unexpected role

Scientists suggest that Jupiter may have played a decisive role in this process. The gas giant likely began forming shortly after the birth of the Sun, possibly within the first million years.

As an enormous disk of gas, dust, and ice surrounded the young star, Jupiter grew rapidly and acted as a kind of barrier. The planet may have blocked the passage of many larger particles, while smaller ones could move around it and mix in the region near the snow line.

This mixture may have given rise to the bodies that eventually became Bennu, Ryugu, and CI meteorites.

This scenario also helps explain why Bennu contains so much water. Some of the ice in the region may have turned into vapor and later condensed again, while Jupiter's influence encouraged the accumulation of fine dust.

A window into Earth's origins

Bennu is particularly valuable because it preserves materials that have remained virtually unchanged since the birth of the solar system. Its composition could provide one of the best available glimpses into the original mixture of chemical elements from which the rocky planets eventually formed.

Its abundance of water and organic matter also makes this small asteroid an important piece of the puzzle in understanding how the young Earth may have received some of the ingredients necessary for life to emerge.

Researchers now want to determine whether other asteroids share the same isotopic signature. They also hope to establish more precisely how much influence the young Jupiter had on the selection of particles that eventually formed these bodies.

The research on Bennu may be nearing its conclusion, but for Schönbächler, the next challenge is already beginning: obtaining samples from Phobos, one of Mars' moons, through Japan's MMX mission. If everything goes according to plan, the spacecraft will launch in late October of this year, with the samples expected to return to Earth in 2031.

The Swiss laboratory will have to wait several years. But the material from Bennu has already made one thing clear: to understand how our cosmic neighborhood formed, sometimes we need to take a very close look at dust that became trapped 4.5 billion years ago.

Article reference

Schoenbaechler M, Ek M, Fehr MA, et al. (2026). Nucleosynthetic constraints on the origin of Bennu and CI-like asteroids.
